title: Evidence that DNA carries genetic information — video support
purpose: Connect each experiment with its observation, control and justified conclusion.
fallback: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty studied transforming preparations and used treatments aimed at different components. When DNA was destroyed, transforming activity was lost. Comparable treatments directed at other components did not remove activity in the same way. This was stronger evidence for DNA because the experiment connected an intervention with the loss of a measured function. The useful comparison is not simply that DNA was present. It is that destroying DNA disrupted transformation under the experimental conditions.

title: DNA structure and complementary strands — video support
purpose: Identify nucleotide components, complementary base pairing and antiparallel strand directions.
fallback: In the standard double-stranded DNA model, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. A and G are double-ring purines; C and T are single-ring pyrimidines. A purine paired with a pyrimidine helps maintain a consistent width. The strands are antiparallel. If an upper strand is written 5′-ATGC-3′, its aligned partner is 3′-TACG-5′. If you must report that partner in the 5′ to 3′ direction, reverse the displayed order: 5′-GCAT-3′. The numbers identify positions in the sugar and therefore strand orientation. They do not identify the first and third bases in a codon. Direction becomes essential when interpreting replication and transcription.

title: DNA replication and its products — video support
purpose: Trace semiconservative replication using base pairing, enzyme roles and the 5′ to 3′ synthesis rule.
fallback: DNA polymerase cannot begin a new strand from nothing. Primase makes a short RNA primer that supplies a starting 3′ end. DNA polymerase then extends from that end with complementary DNA nucleotides. New DNA is always synthesized 5′ to 3′. Because the parental templates run in opposite directions, their new strands cannot both follow the moving replication fork continuously. The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork. The lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments, each extending 5′ to 3′ away from the fork as additional template is exposed. Each fragment requires a primer.

title: Transcription and RNA processing — video support
purpose: Use template and coding strand identities to construct mRNA and explain eukaryotic RNA processing.
fallback: Transcription copies the information of a selected DNA region into RNA. The DNA strands close behind the enzyme and the RNA separates. It does not copy the entire genome in the same way as S-phase replication. Because one continuous RNA molecule is synthesized from one template, transcription does not require a leading strand, lagging strand or Okazaki fragments. Those terms belong to DNA replication at a fork.

title: Translation and the genetic code — video support
purpose: Use mRNA codons, tRNA anticodons and start/stop signals to explain polypeptide synthesis.
fallback: A tRNA carries an amino acid and has an anticodon that can pair with a complementary mRNA codon. The strands pair antiparallel. For mRNA 5′-AUG-3′, an aligned anticodon is 3′-UAC-5′. Ribosomes contain rRNA and proteins. As matching tRNAs enter and the ribosome moves along the mRNA, amino acids are linked by peptide bonds. The growing chain is a polypeptide, which can later fold and undergo additional processing. The mRNA is not physically converted into protein. It is read as information while amino acids are assembled from a separate supply.

title: Solving DNA, RNA and protein problems — video support
purpose: Solve sequence problems by identifying the supplied molecule, direction, frame and requested output.
fallback: For a complete simplified message, begin at the specified start AUG and stop at the first in-frame stop codon. Divide the sequence into triplets only after establishing the start. Such an exercise can ask for amino-acid identities without including the beginning of the protein. Do not invent a start or stop that the question does not provide. A stretch coding for five amino acids contains fifteen coding nucleotides. An additional stop codon requires three more nucleotides but does not add an amino acid. title: Mutations and their effects on proteins — video support
purpose: Distinguish a DNA mutation from expression errors and explain substitution, frameshift and inheritance consequences.
fallback: Consider the internal mRNA coding segment CAG UUA CCC. It specifies Gln–Leu–Pro. Changing UUA to UUG still gives leucine, a silent substitution. Changing UUA to UCA gives serine, a missense change. Changing it to UAA creates a stop signal. The size of a change in DNA does not by itself determine the effect on the organism. Protein location, function, remaining sequence and other biological factors matter. A missense change can be important or relatively minor; a premature stop can remove a critical region.

title: Recombination and sources of variation — video support
purpose: Distinguish mutation, recombination and transfer of existing genetic material.
fallback: Bacteria normally reproduce by binary fission, but they can also acquire DNA from other sources. Transformation involves uptake of external DNA. Conjugation involves direct contact and transfer, often including plasmids. Transduction involves a virus carrying bacterial genetic material. These mechanisms can introduce traits into a bacterial lineage. They are not the same as mitosis or the production and fusion of animal gametes. The important question is how the DNA enters and how it can persist in descendants. A transferred sequence must be maintained and expressed in an appropriate context to affect a phenotype. Detecting DNA outside a cell is not enough to establish a stable inherited change.

title: Recombinant DNA and genetic engineering — video support
purpose: Explain the conceptual roles of restriction enzymes, ligase, vectors and expression in recombinant-DNA technology.
fallback: A transferred gene must be linked to appropriate expression signals and interpreted by the host machinery. Many human genes contain introns. Bacteria do not normally process human introns in the same way as human cells, so a suitable intron-free coding sequence may be used. Complementary DNA, or cDNA, can be made from a processed RNA template. This provides one route to an intron-free sequence. The conceptual point is that the host must receive usable coding information, not just any piece cut from a human chromosome. Production of a human protein in bacteria therefore depends on both the sequence and the expression context. The insulin example illustrates a biological manufacturing principle rather than a complete laboratory protocol.

title: PCR, gels and interpreting DNA profiles — video support
purpose: Explain DNA amplification and fragment separation, then interpret profiles within their limits.
fallback: DNA has a negative charge because of its phosphate backbone. In a standard DNA gel, an electric field draws fragments toward the positive electrode. Smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel than larger fragments under the same conditions. Samples are loaded into separate lanes. A DNA ladder provides fragments of known sizes for comparison. Identify the wells, migration direction and ladder before interpreting a band position. A band represents many molecules of similar length, not one whole cell. Two fragments can have the same length without necessarily having identical sequences.
